Binary safety holds — the stop-everything check passed\n65\t\n66\tZero byte mismatches and zero corrupt tiles across ~6,000 decoded packets. Every\n67\trecovered payload matched its deterministic expansion bit for bit, over payloads\n68\tcontaining the full 0x00–0xFF range. D3's choice of `zxing-wasm` + `.bytes` is\n69\tconfirmed on real hardware, and invariant I10 held.\n70\t\n71\t### 2. ROI cropping is worth 8.6× — but only when there is something to crop\n72\t\n73\tRun 2 cut decode p50 from **56.9 ms to 6.6 ms**, almost exactly the 9× the research\n74\tpredicted. But run 3 shows the nuance the research did *not* state: once the grid\n75\tfills the frame — which is exactly what you want for px/module — the ROI *is* the\n76\tframe, and the win evaporates (69 ms).\n77\t\n78\t> **ROI cropping is a recovery mechanism for being too far away, not a throughput\n79\t> optimisation at the correct distance.** Worth implementing, worth not counting on.\n80\t\n81\tA trap worth recording: the first ROI implementation was a **one-way ratchet**. A\n82\tframe in which only two tiles decoded shrank the crop to those two tiles, so every\n83\tlater frame saw only that region and could never recover the grid — erasure 91%,\n84\tgoodput *worse* than no cropping. Fixed with a 35% margin plus a forced full-frame\n85\trescan every 20 frames. Any ROI implementation in the real app needs the same guard.\n86\t\n87\t### 3. Decode p50 of 67–69 ms exceeds §13.1's ≤ 60 ms budget\n88\t\n89\tOn a full 1080p frame, single-threaded, no worker. This is the binding constraint on\n90\tcamera fps (4.5–6.3 observed), and therefore on everything downstream. The plan\n91\talready specifies the fixes — a worker pool (§6.2) and ROI (§6.4) — and neither is in\n92\tthe rig. **The budget is not yet violated by the design; it is violated by the\n93\tinstrument.**\n94\t\n95\t### 4. The sender is the other bottleneck, and D4 is not optional\n96\t\n97\tThe T450s managed **6.7 fps against 12 requested**, decaying to 2.4 fps over two\n98\tminutes. Per-tile QR encode runs synchronously on the main thread with **no pinned\n99\tmask** — D4 measured that as a 4.6–8× encode speedup and it is unimplemented here.\n100\t§6.3.1's budget of 0.29 ms/tile is not being met by roughly an order of magnitude on\n101\t2015 hardware.\n102\t\n103\t### 5. Run 4 is a live demonstration of why D9 exists\n104\t\n105\tRuns 1–3 emitted **201 packets/s** into a receiver that could absorb at most ~141 —\n106\tthe sender was running **2.8× faster than D9's \"≤ half the measured camera fps\"**\n107\trule allows. Obeying the rule (run 4) cut erasure from 78% to **48%** and drove\n108\tframes-yielding-zero to **0%**.\n109\t\n110\tGoodput fell too, because a slower sender emits less — which is the real lesson:\n111\t**D9 is a constraint to satisfy, not a dial to maximise.** The sender must measure the\n112\treceiver's rate, and it cannot (no back-channel). This is the strongest argument yet\n113\tfor open question 7 and for the §8.2 repair code.\n114\t\n115\t### 6. D14 works on the Pixel 6\n116\t\n117\t`exposureApplied: true`. The capability is present and the constraint applied cleanly.\n118\tIts effect size is not isolated here — a with/without comparison is still owed.\n119\t\n120\t---\n121\t\n122\t## Kill criteria — status\n123\t\n124\tFrom `spike/README.md`, fixed before the runs:\n125\t\n126\t| Criterion | Observed | Verdict |\n127\t|---|---|---|\n128\t| < 10 KB/s laptop→phone (R3) | 11.2 KB/s best | **not tripped**, but uncomfortably close |\n129\t| Erasure > 35% handheld (R9) | 48–78% | **TRIPPED — see below** |\n130\t| GE below required (R1) | 7.1× margin | **not tripped** |\n131\t| Phone→phone yields nothing (R4) | not yet tested | outstanding |\n132\t| R1 rung fails while R3 works | not yet tested | outstanding |\n133\t| **byte mismatches ≠ 0** | **0** | **not tripped** |\n134\t| No cliff, a slope instead | not yet tested | outstanding |\n135\t\n136\t### On the tripped erasure criterion\n137\t\n138\tThe honest reading is that **this does not yet invalidate D18c's 20–30% assumption**,\n139\tbecause the erasure measured here is dominated by *rate mismatch*, not optical loss:\n140\tthe sender was emitting faster than the receiver could sample (§5 above), and in the\n141\tone D9-compliant run erasure fell to 48% and is still falling as conditions improve.\n142\t\n143\tWhat it does establish is that **erasure is the number to watch**, and that D18c\n144\tcannot be left as an assumption. Re-test after: sender in a worker with a pinned mask,\n145\treceiver with a worker pool, tripod mounting, and proper lighting. If erasure is still\n146\tabove 35% under §13.2 conditions, R12's fallback applies — the repair code becomes the\n147\tprimary recovery path, not the tail.\n148\t\n149\t---\n150\t\n151\t## Plan changes this justifies\n152\t\n153\tNothing here changes a decision yet — the setup deviates too far from §13.2. It does\n154\tchange confidence and priority:\n155\t\n156\t1. **§18 R1 → Low.** GE is not the constraint. Close it properly with an on-device run.\n157\t2. **Decode cost is the near-term risk, not fountain cost.** The worker pool (§6.2) and\n158\t   ROI (§6.4) move from \"planned\" to \"load-bearing for Phase 3's ≥20 KB/s\".\n159\t3. **D4's pinned mask is on the critical path**, not an optimisation — the sender\n160\t   cannot hold frame rate without it on older hardware.\n161\t4. **Add the ROI ratchet guard** to §6.4 as an anti-pattern; it silently made things\n162\t   worse in a way that looked like an optical problem.\n163\t5. **D9 needs a measured input the sender does not have.** Strengthens open question 7.\n164\t\n165\t---\n166\t\n167\t## Still outstanding\n168\t\n169\t- S3 distance sweep (the px/module cliff) — **the most valuable unrun test**\n170\t- S4 phone→phone (R4)\n171\t- Rung sweep R1→R4\n172\t- With/without `exposureCompensation` comparison\n173\t- On-device GE benchmark\n174\t- Everything under §13.2 conditions, ≥ 5 trials, median reported\n175\t\n176\t---\n177\t\n178\t# S3 — density sweep: what actually limits throughput\n179\t\n180\tRun after the question \"is there something denser than QR?\" — the answer turned out\n181\tto be no, or at least not yet, and the measurements say why.\n182\t\n183\t## The correction that reframes everything\n184\t\n185\t**The 4 px/module cliff is measured in CAMERA pixels, not screen pixels.** The plan\n186\tand the rig both used \"module px\" to mean screen pixels, and the two differ by the\n187\tratio of capture width to the screen's width in frame.\n188\t\n189\tThe Pixel 6 was capturing **1080×1920 portrait** while the sender's screen is\n190\t**1920×1080 landscape**, so the screen's long axis landed on the camera's *short*\n191\taxis: 1080 / 1920 = **0.5625×**. Four screen px/module was therefore **2.25 camera\n192\tpx/module — well below the cliff.**\n193\t\n194\tThat single fact explains the 48–78% erasure from S2. We were not measuring a\n195\tsymbology limit. We were measuring a sampling limit.\n196\t\n197\t## The cliff, measured\n198\t\n199\tCapture resolution swept at fixed geometry (R2, 4 screen px/module, 15 tiles, sender 3 fps):\n200\t\n201\t| Capture | Camera px/module | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput | Frames w/ zero |\n202\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n203\t| 720×1280 | **1.50** | 8.9 | 33 ms | **100%** | 0.0 KB/s | **100%** |\n204\t| 1080×1920 | **2.25** | 4.4 | 22 ms | 78% | **4.0 KB/s** | 1% |\n205\t| 1440×2560 | **3.00** | 2.5 | 42 ms | 88% | 2.1 KB/s | 2% |\n206\t| 2160×3840 | **4.50** | 1.1 | 194 ms | — | 3.4 KB/s | **0%** |\n207\t\n208\tTwo things are visible and neither is about QR:\n209\t\n210\t1. **It is a cliff, not a slope.** At 1.5 camera px/module *nothing* decodes — 100%\n211\t   erasure, every frame empty. At 2.25 it works badly. The research's characterisation\n212\t   is confirmed on real hardware.\n213\t2. **Raising capture resolution does not help by itself.** Decode is O(pixels), so 4K\n214\t   bought optical health (zero empty frames) and paid for it with 194 ms decode and\n215\t   1.1 fps — net *worse* goodput. There is a knee, and at this geometry it sits near\n216\t   1080×1920.\n217\t\n218\t`byteMismatches: 0` in every run, including the 100%-erasure one. The erasure channel\n219\tproperty holds even when the channel delivers nothing at all.\n220\t\n221\t## The free 1.78× nobody is taking\n222\t\n223\tThe phone is physically **portrait** while the screen is **landscape**, so 44% of the\n224\tsensor images nothing useful. Physically rotating the phone 90° puts the screen's long\n225\taxis on the camera's long axis: **1.78× more camera pixels on the code, at identical\n226\tdecode cost.** That is a bigger win than any symbology change on the table, and it\n227\tcosts nothing.\n228\t\n229\tVerified negative: setting Android's `user_rotation` to landscape does **not** do it —\n230\tcapture stayed 1080×1920 and camera px/module stayed 2.25. The sensor mapping follows\n231\tthe device body, not the UI orientation. This needs a physical rotation (or a mount).\n232\t\n233\t## QR is denser per pixel than libcimbar\n234\t\n235\tWorth recording because it contradicts the framing the plan inherited:\n236\t\n237\t| Scheme | Bits per screen px² |\n238\t|---|---|\n239\t| libcimbar, 6 bits/cell over 9×9 px | 0.0741 |\n240\t| **QR v16-L at 3 px/module** | **0.0794** |\n241\t| QR v16-L at 2 px/module | 0.1786 |\n242\t\n243\t**libcimbar's 106 KB/s is not a density win — it is a frame-rate win.** It sustains\n244\t~11 decoded frames/s where we manage 2–4. That reorders the plan's Stage 2/Stage 3\n245\targument: the custom codec's value is decode *speed* per bit, not bits per pixel.\n246\t\n247\t## What 1 Mbps needs\n248\t\n249\t125 KB/s, from the measured constraints. Requires camera px/module ≥ 4 *and* enough\n250\tbits/frame *and* enough frame rate:\n251\t\n252\t| Configuration | Cam px/module | KB/frame | Sender fps needed |\n253\t|---|---|---|---|\n254\t| portrait @ 4 screen px/mod (today) | 2.25 ✗ | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n255\t| **landscape @ 4 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n256\t| landscape @ 3 screen px/mod | 3.00 ✗ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n257\t| **landscape 4K @ 2 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | **37.8** | **3.3** |\n258\t| landscape 4K @ 3 screen px/mod | 6.00 ✓ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n259\t\n260\tThe bottom row is the interesting one: **at 4K landscape and 2 screen px/module, 1 Mbps\n261\tneeds only 3.3 sender fps** — slower than the 6.7 fps the 2015 bench laptop already\n262\tmanages. The density is not the problem.\n263\t\n264\tWhat stands between here and there, in order of value:\n265\t\n266\t1. **Physically rotate the phone to landscape** — 1.78×, free, no code.\n267\t2. **Tight ROI crop to the screen quad** — at 4K the screen is a fraction of the frame;\n268\t   decoding only it keeps px/module high *and* pixel count bounded. This is what makes\n269\t   4K affordable, and the current ROI (35% margin, full-frame rescans) is far too loose.\n270\t3. **Decode in a worker pool** (§6.2) — decode currently gates camera fps directly.\n271\t4. **D4's pinned mask on the sender** — needed to hold ≥ 8 fps on modest hardware.\n272\t5. **Only then** revisit colour or a custom codec, against a receiver that is not\n273\t   CPU-starved.\n274\t\n275\t**1 Mbps is roughly libcimbar's demonstrated 850 kbps, so it sits at the edge of what\n276\tcommodity hardware has ever shown.** Nothing measured here says it is unreachable, and\n277\tnothing measured here says a denser symbology is the way to reach it.\n278\t\n279\t## Revised answer to \"is there something denser than QR?\"\n280\t\n281\tNot usefully, at this stage. The measured limits are, in order:\n282\t\n283\t1. camera px/module (below the cliff — fixable free, by rotation)\n284\t2. decode CPU (fixable with a worker pool and a tight ROI)\n285\t3. sender encode CPU (fixable with D4's pinned mask)\n286\t4. …and only then symbology density\n287\t\n288\tItems 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is\n289\tthe last lever to pull, not the first.\n290\t\n291\t---\n292\t\n293\t# Thermal — the finding that most threatens the premise\n294\t\n295\tFlagged by the operator mid-session: *\"the phone itself is also getting exceptionally\n296\twarm.\"* Confirmed on the device immediately after stopping:\n297\t\n298\t| Sensor | Reading |\n299\t|---|---|\n300\t| CPU (LITTLE cluster) | **70.0 °C** |\n301\t| `quiet_therm` | 34.1 °C, **`mStatus=1` — throttling threshold reached** |\n302\t| Battery | 34.1 °C |\n303\t| Display | 35.9 °C |\n304\t\n305\tThis was after roughly **20–30 minutes** of intermittent decoding, much of it at 1080p\n306\tand some at 4K, on an unmounted phone with no airflow.\n307\t\n308\t## Why this matters more than any throughput number\n309\t\n310\tThe plan's headline objective is multi-gigabyte transfer. §1.1 states 10 GB is\n311\t**27 hours to 4 days** of *continuous* decoding. A receiver that reaches its throttling\n312\tthreshold in under half an hour cannot do that, and no amount of coding efficiency\n313\tfixes it.\n314\t\n315\tWorse, thermal throttling is **self-reinforcing on this channel**: the SoC slows →\n316\tdecode latency rises → camera fps falls → erasure rises → the transfer takes longer →\n317\tmore total heat. The plan already names the mechanism in edge case E17 and risk R9, but\n318\tboth assumed it was an *hours* problem. It is a *tens of minutes* problem.\n319\t\n320\tAlso invalidating: **every measurement in S2/S3 was taken on a device that was heating\n321\tthroughout.** Later runs are not comparable to earlier ones, which is an additional\n322\treason (beyond §13.2 deviations) that none of these figures are budget-qualifying. A\n323\tproper campaign needs cool-down between runs and a recorded starting temperature.\n324\t\n325\t## What this changes\n326\t\n327\t**Continuous full-rate decoding is not a viable operating mode for long transfers.**\n328\tThe design needs a thermal strategy, not a thermal warning. Options, cheapest first:\n329\t\n330\t1. **Duty-cycle the receiver.** Decode a burst, idle, repeat. On a fountain-coded\n331\t   erasure channel this is nearly free — skipped frames are erasures, which the code\n332\t   already absorbs. A 50% duty cycle roughly halves heat for roughly half the rate,\n333\t   and *finishes* where 100% duty may not.\n334\t2. **Drop the decode resolution under thermal pressure**, rather than dropping frames.\n335\t   Fewer pixels is superlinearly cheaper.\n336\t3. **Read the thermal state and adapt.** No web API exposes SoC temperature, but\n337\t   sustained fps decline is a usable proxy — the same signal E17 already proposes.\n338\t4. **Design the UX around it**: a 10 GB transfer becomes a series of sessions with\n339\t   cool-downs, which the resume machinery (D22) already supports. This may be the\n340\t   honest framing rather than a defect.\n341\t\n342\t## New risk\n343\t\n344\t**R11 — thermal throttling makes long transfers self-defeating.** Likelihood **High**\n345\t(observed in the first session). Impact **High** (attacks the multi-GB objective\n346\tdirectly). Mitigation: duty-cycling (above) plus resume. Trigger: sustained fps decline\n347\t> 30% from a cool start → drop duty cycle and tell the user, rather than silently\n348\trunning hot and slow.\n349\t\n350\tThis should be measured properly: a long-run thermal profile with cool-down, plotting\n351\tdecode latency and camera fps against elapsed time. The capability is present and the constraint applied cleanly.\nIts effect size is not isolated here — a with/without comparison is still owed.\n\n---\n\n## Kill criteria — status\n\nFrom `spike/README.md`, fixed before the runs:\n\n| Criterion | Observed | Verdict |\n|---|---|---|\n| < 10 KB/s laptop→phone (R3) | 11.2 KB/s best | **not tripped**, but uncomfortably close |\n| Erasure > 35% handheld (R9) | 48–78% | **TRIPPED — see below** |\n| GE below required (R1) | 7.1× margin | **not tripped** |\n| Phone→phone yields nothing (R4) | not yet tested | outstanding |\n| R1 rung fails while R3 works | not yet tested | outstanding |\n| **byte mismatches ≠ 0** | **0** | **not tripped** |\n| No cliff, a slope instead | not yet tested | outstanding |\n\n### On the tripped erasure criterion\n\nThe honest reading is that **this does not yet invalidate D18c's 20–30% assumption**,\nbecause the erasure measured here is dominated by *rate mismatch*, not optical loss:\nthe sender was emitting faster than the receiver could sample (§5 above), and in the\none D9-compliant run erasure fell to 48% and is still falling as conditions improve.\n\nWhat it does establish is that **erasure is the number to watch**, and that D18c\ncannot be left as an assumption. Re-test after: sender in a worker with a pinned mask,\nreceiver with a worker pool, tripod mounting, and proper lighting. If erasure is still\nabove 35% under §13.2 conditions, R12's fallback applies — the repair code becomes the\nprimary recovery path, not the tail.\n\n---\n\n## Plan changes this justifies\n\nNothing here changes a decision yet — the setup deviates too far from §13.2. It does\nchange confidence and priority:\n\n1. **§18 R1 → Low.** GE is not the constraint. Close it properly with an on-device run.\n2. **Decode cost is the near-term risk, not fountain cost.** The worker pool (§6.2) and\n   ROI (§6.4) move from \"planned\" to \"load-bearing for Phase 3's ≥20 KB/s\".\n3. **D4's pinned mask is on the critical path**, not an optimisation — the sender\n   cannot hold frame rate without it on older hardware.\n4. **Add the ROI ratchet guard** to §6.4 as an anti-pattern; it silently made things\n   worse in a way that looked like an optical problem.\n5. **D9 needs a measured input the sender does not have.** Strengthens open question 7.\n\n---\n\n## Still outstanding\n\n- S3 distance sweep (the px/module cliff) — **the most valuable unrun test**\n- S4 phone→phone (R4)\n- Rung sweep R1→R4\n- With/without `exposureCompensation` comparison\n- On-device GE benchmark\n- Everything under §13.2 conditions, ≥ 5 trials, median reported\n\n---\n\n# S3 — density sweep: what actually limits throughput\n\nRun after the question \"is there something denser than QR?\" — the answer turned out\nto be no, or at least not yet, and the measurements say why.\n\n## The correction that reframes everything\n\n**The 4 px/module cliff is measured in CAMERA pixels, not screen pixels.** The plan\nand the rig both used \"module px\" to mean screen pixels, and the two differ by the\nratio of capture width to the screen's width in frame.\n\nThe Pixel 6 was capturing **1080×1920 portrait** while the sender's screen is\n**1920×1080 landscape**, so the screen's long axis landed on the camera's *short*\naxis: 1080 / 1920 = **0.5625×**. Four screen px/module was therefore **2.25 camera\npx/module — well below the cliff.**\n\nThat single fact explains the 48–78% erasure from S2. We were not measuring a\nsymbology limit. We were measuring a sampling limit.\n\n## The cliff, measured\n\nCapture resolution swept at fixed geometry (R2, 4 screen px/module, 15 tiles, sender 3 fps):\n\n| Capture | Camera px/module | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput | Frames w/ zero |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 720×1280 | **1.50** | 8.9 | 33 ms | **100%** | 0.0 KB/s | **100%** |\n| 1080×1920 | **2.25** | 4.4 | 22 ms | 78% | **4.0 KB/s** | 1% |\n| 1440×2560 | **3.00** | 2.5 | 42 ms | 88% | 2.1 KB/s | 2% |\n| 2160×3840 | **4.50** | 1.1 | 194 ms | — | 3.4 KB/s | **0%** |\n\nTwo things are visible and neither is about QR:\n\n1. **It is a cliff, not a slope.** At 1.5 camera px/module *nothing* decodes — 100%\n   erasure, every frame empty. At 2.25 it works badly. The research's characterisation\n   is confirmed on real hardware.\n2. **Raising capture resolution does not help by itself.** Decode is O(pixels), so 4K\n   bought optical health (zero empty frames) and paid for it with 194 ms decode and\n   1.1 fps — net *worse* goodput. There is a knee, and at this geometry it sits near\n   1080×1920.\n\n`byteMismatches: 0` in every run, including the 100%-erasure one. The erasure channel\nproperty holds even when the channel delivers nothing at all.\n\n## The free 1.78× nobody is taking\n\nThe phone is physically **portrait** while the screen is **landscape**, so 44% of the\nsensor images nothing useful. Physically rotating the phone 90° puts the screen's long\naxis on the camera's long axis: **1.78× more camera pixels on the code, at identical\ndecode cost.** That is a bigger win than any symbology change on the table, and it\ncosts nothing.\n\nVerified negative: setting Android's `user_rotation` to landscape does **not** do it —\ncapture stayed 1080×1920 and camera px/module stayed 2.25. The sensor mapping follows\nthe device body, not the UI orientation. This needs a physical rotation (or a mount).\n\n## QR is denser per pixel than libcimbar\n\nWorth recording because it contradicts the framing the plan inherited:\n\n| Scheme | Bits per screen px² |\n|---|---|\n| libcimbar, 6 bits/cell over 9×9 px | 0.0741 |\n| **QR v16-L at 3 px/module** | **0.0794** |\n| QR v16-L at 2 px/module | 0.1786 |\n\n**libcimbar's 106 KB/s is not a density win — it is a frame-rate win.** It sustains\n~11 decoded frames/s where we manage 2–4. That reorders the plan's Stage 2/Stage 3\nargument: the custom codec's value is decode *speed* per bit, not bits per pixel.\n\n## What 1 Mbps needs\n\n125 KB/s, from the measured constraints. Requires camera px/module ≥ 4 *and* enough\nbits/frame *and* enough frame rate:\n\n| Configuration | Cam px/module | KB/frame | Sender fps needed |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| portrait @ 4 screen px/mod (today) | 2.25 ✗ | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n| **landscape @ 4 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n| landscape @ 3 screen px/mod | 3.00 ✗ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n| **landscape 4K @ 2 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | **37.8** | **3.3** |\n| landscape 4K @ 3 screen px/mod | 6.00 ✓ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n\nThe bottom row is the interesting one: **at 4K landscape and 2 screen px/module, 1 Mbps\nneeds only 3.3 sender fps** — slower than the 6.7 fps the 2015 bench laptop already\nmanages. The density is not the problem.\n\nWhat stands between here and there, in order of value:\n\n1. **Physically rotate the phone to landscape** — 1.78×, free, no code.\n2. **Tight ROI crop to the screen quad** — at 4K the screen is a fraction of the frame;\n   decoding only it keeps px/module high *and* pixel count bounded. This is what makes\n   4K affordable, and the current ROI (35% margin, full-frame rescans) is far too loose.\n3. **Decode in a worker pool** (§6.2) — decode currently gates camera fps directly.\n4. **D4's pinned mask on the sender** — needed to hold ≥ 8 fps on modest hardware.\n5. **Only then** revisit colour or a custom codec, against a receiver that is not\n   CPU-starved.\n\n**1 Mbps is roughly libcimbar's demonstrated 850 kbps, so it sits at the edge of what\ncommodity hardware has ever shown.** Nothing measured here says it is unreachable, and\nnothing measured here says a denser symbology is the way to reach it.\n\n## Revised answer to \"is there something denser than QR?\"\n\nNot usefully, at this stage. The measured limits are, in order:\n\n1. camera px/module (below the cliff — fixable free, by rotation)\n2. decode CPU (fixable with a worker pool and a tight ROI)\n3. sender encode CPU (fixable with D4's pinned mask)\n4. …and only then symbology density\n\nItems 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is\nthe last lever to pull, not the first.\n\n---\n\n# Thermal — the finding that most threatens the premise\n\nFlagged by the operator mid-session: *\"the phone itself is also getting exceptionally\nwarm.\"* Confirmed on the device immediately after stopping:\n\n| Sensor | Reading |\n|---|---|\n| CPU (LITTLE cluster) | **70.0 °C** |\n| `quiet_therm` | 34.1 °C, **`mStatus=1` — throttling threshold reached** |\n| Battery | 34.1 °C |\n| Display | 35.9 °C |\n\nThis was after roughly **20–30 minutes** of intermittent decoding, much of it at 1080p\nand some at 4K, on an unmounted phone with no airflow.\n\n## Why this matters more than any throughput number\n\nThe plan's headline objective is multi-gigabyte transfer. §1.1 states 10 GB is\n**27 hours to 4 days** of *continuous* decoding. A receiver that reaches its throttling\nthreshold in under half an hour cannot do that, and no amount of coding efficiency\nfixes it.\n\nWorse, thermal throttling is **self-reinforcing on this channel**: the SoC slows →\ndecode latency rises → camera fps falls → erasure rises → the transfer takes longer →\nmore total heat. The plan already names the mechanism in edge case E17 and risk R9, but\nboth assumed it was an *hours* problem. It is a *tens of minutes* problem.\n\nAlso invalidating: **every measurement in S2/S3 was taken on a device that was heating\nthroughout.** Later runs are not comparable to earlier ones, which is an additional\nreason (beyond §13.2 deviations) that none of these figures are budget-qualifying. A\nproper campaign needs cool-down between runs and a recorded starting temperature.\n\n## What this changes\n\n**Continuous full-rate decoding is not a viable operating mode for long transfers.**\nThe design needs a thermal strategy, not a thermal warning. Options, cheapest first:\n\n1. **Duty-cycle the receiver.** Decode a burst, idle, repeat. On a fountain-coded\n   erasure channel this is nearly free — skipped frames are erasures, which the code\n   already absorbs. A 50% duty cycle roughly halves heat for roughly half the rate,\n   and *finishes* where 100% duty may not.\n2. **Drop the decode resolution under thermal pressure**, rather than dropping frames.\n   Fewer pixels is superlinearly cheaper.\n3. **Read the thermal state and adapt.** No web API exposes SoC temperature, but\n   sustained fps decline is a usable proxy — the same signal E17 already proposes.\n4. **Design the UX around it**: a 10 GB transfer becomes a series of sessions with\n   cool-downs, which the resume machinery (D22) already supports. This may be the\n   honest framing rather than a defect.\n\n## New risk\n\n**R11 — thermal throttling makes long transfers self-defeating.** Likelihood **High**\n(observed in the first session). Impact **High** (attacks the multi-GB objective\ndirectly). Mitigation: duty-cycling (above) plus resume. Trigger: sustained fps decline\n> 30% from a cool start → drop duty cycle and tell the user, rather than silently\nrunning hot and slow.\n\nThis should be measured properly: a long-run thermal profile with cool-down, plotting\ndecode latency and camera fps against elapsed time. It is the single most important\noutstanding measurement, ahead of any density work.\n","numLines":353,"startLine":1,"totalLines":353}}}

Recorded per the ground rules\nin [`spike/README.md`](../../spike/README.md): write the numbers down even when they\nare good, and never quote one without its denominator.\n\n**Headline: the optical loop works end to end, and byte-exactness held in every run.\nThroughput is below target, but the conditions were far from the reference setup and\ntwo sender-side optimisations the plan already specifies are not yet implemented.**\n\n---\n\n## Setup (the denominator — §13.2)\n\n| Parameter | Value | Reference (§13.2) | Deviation |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Sender | Lenovo T450s (2015, Broadwell i5), 1920×1080, chromium | 1080p, 50%+ brightness | older/slower than typical |\n| Receiver | Pixel 6, rear camera, Chrome | mid-range Android | matches |\n| Mounting | **hand-placed, not mounted** | tripod for budget figures | ✗ |\n| Lighting | dim room, screen is the only source | ~300 lux | ✗ |\n| Distance | ~30–40 cm, uncalibrated | 30 cm measured | approximate |\n| Rung | R2 (v16, 2 packets/tile), 4 px/module | — | — |\n| Grid | **5×3 = 15 tiles**, auto-fitted to 1920×1080 | — | matches the plan's 15 |\n| Trials | 1 per configuration | ≥ 5, report median | ✗ |\n\n**These are not budget-qualifying measurements.** Three of the seven parameters\ndeviate from §13.2, so none of these numbers may be quoted as a §13.1 result. They\nare directional, and that is enough to act on.\n\n---\n\n## S1 — GE decode throughput (no camera)\n\n`node spike/ge-bench.mjs` — full GF(2) elimination of one block, not a synthetic XOR loop.\n\n| K | Block | Decode | Throughput | Est. phone (÷4) | Stage 3 margin |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **768** | 192 KB | **8 ms** | **3,260 MB/s** | 815 MB/s | **7.11×** |\n| 1152 | 288 KB | 20 ms | 3,204 MB/s | 801 MB/s | 4.10× |\n\n**R1 provisionally closed.** The plan's 200 MB/s phone-JS budget was ~16× pessimistic\non desktop. Still to do: run this in a browser *on the Pixel 6* — the ÷4 factor is a\nguess, and thermal behaviour over a multi-hour transfer is unmeasured.\n\n---\n\n## S2 — optical loop, R2 at 4 px/module, 15 tiles\n\nThree runs, each ~50 s, each fixing a defect the previous one exposed.\n\n| # | Change | Sender fps | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | baseline, full-frame decode | 6.7 | 4.5 | **56.9 ms** | — | 6.6 KB/s |\n| 2 | + ROI crop | 6.7 | 6.3 | **6.6 ms** | 91% | 4.6 KB/s |\n| 3 | + ROI ratchet fix | 6.7 | 4.7 | 69.2 ms | 78% | **11.2 KB/s** |\n| 4 | + D9-compliant sender rate | 2.0 | 4.5 | 67.0 ms | **48%** | 7.0 KB/s |\n\n**In every run: `byteMismatches: 0` and `corruptTiles: 0`.**\n\n---\n\n## What the numbers say\n\n### 1. Binary safety holds — the stop-everything check passed\n\nZero byte mismatches and zero corrupt tiles across ~6,000 decoded packets. Every\nrecovered payload matched its deterministic expansion bit for bit, over payloads\ncontaining the full 0x00–0xFF range. D3's choice of `zxing-wasm` + `.bytes` is\nconfirmed on real hardware, and invariant I10 held.\n\n### 2. ROI cropping is worth 8.6× — but only when there is something to crop\n\nRun 2 cut decode p50 from **56.9 ms to 6.6 ms**, almost exactly the 9× the research\npredicted. But run 3 shows the nuance the research did *not* state: once the grid\nfills the frame — which is exactly what you want for px/module — the ROI *is* the\nframe, and the win evaporates (69 ms).\n\n> **ROI cropping is a recovery mechanism for being too far away, not a throughput\n> optimisation at the correct distance.** Worth implementing, worth not counting on.\n\nA trap worth recording: the first ROI implementation was a **one-way ratchet**. A\nframe in which only two tiles decoded shrank the crop to those two tiles, so every\nlater frame saw only that region and could never recover the grid — erasure 91%,\ngoodput *worse* than no cropping. Fixed with a 35% margin plus a forced full-frame\nrescan every 20 frames. Any ROI implementation in the real app needs the same guard.\n\n### 3. Decode p50 of 67–69 ms exceeds §13.1's ≤ 60 ms budget\n\nOn a full 1080p frame, single-threaded, no worker. This is the binding constraint on\ncamera fps (4.5–6.3 observed), and therefore on everything downstream. The plan\nalready specifies the fixes — a worker pool (§6.2) and ROI (§6.4) — and neither is in\nthe rig. **The budget is not yet violated by the design; it is violated by the\ninstrument.**\n\n### 4. The sender is the other bottleneck, and D4 is not optional\n\nThe T450s managed **6.7 fps against 12 requested**, decaying to 2.4 fps over two\nminutes. Per-tile QR encode runs synchronously on the main thread with **no pinned\nmask** — D4 measured that as a 4.6–8× encode speedup and it is unimplemented here.\n§6.3.1's budget of 0.29 ms/tile is not being met by roughly an order of magnitude on\n2015 hardware.\n\n### 5. Run 4 is a live demonstration of why D9 exists\n\nRuns 1–3 emitted **201 packets/s** into a receiver that could absorb at most ~141 —\nthe sender was running **2.8× faster than D9's \"≤ half the measured camera fps\"**\nrule allows. Obeying the rule (run 4) cut erasure from 78% to **48%** and drove\nframes-yielding-zero to **0%**.\n\nGoodput fell too, because a slower sender emits less — which is the real lesson:\n**D9 is a constraint to satisfy, not a dial to maximise.** The sender must measure the\nreceiver's rate, and it cannot (no back-channel). This is the strongest argument yet\nfor open question 7 and for the §8.2 repair code.\n\n### 6. D14 works on the Pixel 6\n\n`exposureApplied: true`. The capability is present and the constraint applied cleanly.\nIts effect size is not isolated here — a with/without comparison is still owed.\n\n---\n\n## Kill criteria — status\n\nFrom `spike/README.md`, fixed before the runs:\n\n| Criterion | Observed | Verdict |\n|---|---|---|\n| < 10 KB/s laptop→phone (R3) | 11.2 KB/s best | **not tripped**, but uncomfortably close |\n| Erasure > 35% handheld (R9) | 48–78% | **TRIPPED — see below** |\n| GE below required (R1) | 7.1× margin | **not tripped** |\n| Phone→phone yields nothing (R4) | not yet tested | outstanding |\n| R1 rung fails while R3 works | not yet tested | outstanding |\n| **byte mismatches ≠ 0** | **0** | **not tripped** |\n| No cliff, a slope instead | not yet tested | outstanding |\n\n### On the tripped erasure criterion\n\nThe honest reading is that **this does not yet invalidate D18c's 20–30% assumption**,\nbecause the erasure measured here is dominated by *rate mismatch*, not optical loss:\nthe sender was emitting faster than the receiver could sample (§5 above), and in the\none D9-compliant run erasure fell to 48% and is still falling as conditions improve.\n\nWhat it does establish is that **erasure is the number to watch**, and that D18c\ncannot be left as an assumption. Re-test after: sender in a worker with a pinned mask,\nreceiver with a worker pool, tripod mounting, and proper lighting. If erasure is still\nabove 35% under §13.2 conditions, R12's fallback applies — the repair code becomes the\nprimary recovery path, not the tail.\n\n---\n\n## Plan changes this justifies\n\nNothing here changes a decision yet — the setup deviates too far from §13.2. It does\nchange confidence and priority:\n\n1. **§18 R1 → Low.** GE is not the constraint. Close it properly with an on-device run.\n2. **Decode cost is the near-term risk, not fountain cost.** The worker pool (§6.2) and\n   ROI (§6.4) move from \"planned\" to \"load-bearing for Phase 3's ≥20 KB/s\".\n3. **D4's pinned mask is on the critical path**, not an optimisation — the sender\n   cannot hold frame rate without it on older hardware.\n4. **Add the ROI ratchet guard** to §6.4 as an anti-pattern; it silently made things\n   worse in a way that looked like an optical problem.\n5. **D9 needs a measured input the sender does not have.** Strengthens open question 7.\n\n---\n\n## Still outstanding\n\n- S3 distance sweep (the px/module cliff) — **the most valuable unrun test**\n- S4 phone→phone (R4)\n- Rung sweep R1→R4\n- With/without `exposureCompensation` comparison\n- On-device GE benchmark\n- Everything under §13.2 conditions, ≥ 5 trials, median reported\n\n---\n\n# S3 — density sweep: what actually limits throughput\n\nRun after the question \"is there something denser than QR?\" — the answer turned out\nto be no, or at least not yet, and the measurements say why.\n\n## The correction that reframes everything\n\n**The 4 px/module cliff is measured in CAMERA pixels, not screen pixels.** The plan\nand the rig both used \"module px\" to mean screen pixels, and the two differ by the\nratio of capture width to the screen's width in frame.\n\nThe Pixel 6 was capturing **1080×1920 portrait** while the sender's screen is\n**1920×1080 landscape**, so the screen's long axis landed on the camera's *short*\naxis: 1080 / 1920 = **0.5625×**. Four screen px/module was therefore **2.25 camera\npx/module — well below the cliff.**\n\nThat single fact explains the 48–78% erasure from S2. We were not measuring a\nsymbology limit. We were measuring a sampling limit.\n\n## The cliff, measured\n\nCapture resolution swept at fixed geometry (R2, 4 screen px/module, 15 tiles, sender 3 fps):\n\n| Capture | Camera px/module | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput | Frames w/ zero |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 720×1280 | **1.50** | 8.9 | 33 ms | **100%** | 0.0 KB/s | **100%** |\n| 1080×1920 | **2.25** | 4.4 | 22 ms | 78% | **4.0 KB/s** | 1% |\n| 1440×2560 | **3.00** | 2.5 | 42 ms | 88% | 2.1 KB/s | 2% |\n| 2160×3840 | **4.50** | 1.1 | 194 ms | — | 3.4 KB/s | **0%** |\n\nTwo things are visible and neither is about QR:\n\n1. **It is a cliff, not a slope.** At 1.5 camera px/module *nothing* decodes — 100%\n   erasure, every frame empty. At 2.25 it works badly. The research's characterisation\n   is confirmed on real hardware.\n2. **Raising capture resolution does not help by itself.** Decode is O(pixels), so 4K\n   bought optical health (zero empty frames) and paid for it with 194 ms decode and\n   1.1 fps — net *worse* goodput. There is a knee, and at this geometry it sits near\n   1080×1920.\n\n`byteMismatches: 0` in every run, including the 100%-erasure one. The erasure channel\nproperty holds even when the channel delivers nothing at all.\n\n## The free 1.78× nobody is taking\n\nThe phone is physically **portrait** while the screen is **landscape**, so 44% of the\nsensor images nothing useful. Physically rotating the phone 90° puts the screen's long\naxis on the camera's long axis: **1.78× more camera pixels on the code, at identical\ndecode cost.** That is a bigger win than any symbology change on the table, and it\ncosts nothing.\n\nVerified negative: setting Android's `user_rotation` to landscape does **not** do it —\ncapture stayed 1080×1920 and camera px/module stayed 2.25. The sensor mapping follows\nthe device body, not the UI orientation. This needs a physical rotation (or a mount).\n\n## QR is denser per pixel than libcimbar\n\nWorth recording because it contradicts the framing the plan inherited:\n\n| Scheme | Bits per screen px² |\n|---|---|\n| libcimbar, 6 bits/cell over 9×9 px | 0.0741 |\n| **QR v16-L at 3 px/module** | **0.0794** |\n| QR v16-L at 2 px/module | 0.1786 |\n\n**libcimbar's 106 KB/s is not a density win — it is a frame-rate win.** It sustains\n~11 decoded frames/s where we manage 2–4. That reorders the plan's Stage 2/Stage 3\nargument: the custom codec's value is decode *speed* per bit, not bits per pixel.\n\n## What 1 Mbps needs\n\n125 KB/s, from the measured constraints. Requires camera px/module ≥ 4 *and* enough\nbits/frame *and* enough frame rate:\n\n| Configuration | Cam px/module | KB/frame | Sender fps needed |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| portrait @ 4 screen px/mod (today) | 2.25 ✗ | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n| **landscape @ 4 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n| landscape @ 3 screen px/mod | 3.00 ✗ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n| **landscape 4K @ 2 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | **37.8** | **3.3** |\n| landscape 4K @ 3 screen px/mod | 6.00 ✓ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n\nThe bottom row is the interesting one: **at 4K landscape and 2 screen px/module, 1 Mbps\nneeds only 3.3 sender fps** — slower than the 6.7 fps the 2015 bench laptop already\nmanages. The density is not the problem.\n\nWhat stands between here and there, in order of value:\n\n1. **Physically rotate the phone to landscape** — 1.78×, free, no code.\n2. **Tight ROI crop to the screen quad** — at 4K the screen is a fraction of the frame;\n   decoding only it keeps px/module high *and* pixel count bounded. This is what makes\n   4K affordable, and the current ROI (35% margin, full-frame rescans) is far too loose.\n3. **Decode in a worker pool** (§6.2) — decode currently gates camera fps directly.\n4. **D4's pinned mask on the sender** — needed to hold ≥ 8 fps on modest hardware.\n5. **Only then** revisit colour or a custom codec, against a receiver that is not\n   CPU-starved.\n\n**1 Mbps is roughly libcimbar's demonstrated 850 kbps, so it sits at the edge of what\ncommodity hardware has ever shown.** Nothing measured here says it is unreachable, and\nnothing measured here says a denser symbology is the way to reach it.\n\n## Revised answer to \"is there something denser than QR?\"\n\nNot usefully, at this stage. The measured limits are, in order:\n\n1. camera px/module (below the cliff — fixable free, by rotation)\n2. decode CPU (fixable with a worker pool and a tight ROI)\n3. sender encode CPU (fixable with D4's pinned mask)\n4. …and only then symbology density\n\nItems 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is\nthe last lever to pull, not the first.\n\n---\n\n# Thermal — the finding that most threatens the premise\n\nFlagged by the operator mid-session: *\"the phone itself is also getting exceptionally\nwarm.\"* Confirmed on the device immediately after stopping:\n\n| Sensor | Reading |\n|---|---|\n| CPU (LITTLE cluster) | **70.0 °C** |\n| `quiet_therm` | 34.1 °C, **`mStatus=1` — throttling threshold reached** |\n| Battery | 34.1 °C |\n| Display | 35.9 °C |\n\nThis was after roughly **20–30 minutes** of intermittent decoding, much of it at 1080p\nand some at 4K, on an unmounted phone with no airflow.\n\n## Why this matters more than any throughput number\n\nThe plan's headline objective is multi-gigabyte transfer. §1.1 states 10 GB is\n**27 hours to 4 days** of *continuous* decoding. A receiver that reaches its throttling\nthreshold in under half an hour cannot do that, and no amount of coding efficiency\nfixes it.\n\nWorse, thermal throttling is **self-reinforcing on this channel**: the SoC slows →\ndecode latency rises → camera fps falls → erasure rises → the transfer takes longer →\nmore total heat. The plan already names the mechanism in edge case E17 and risk R9, but\nboth assumed it was an *hours* problem. It is a *tens of minutes* problem.\n\nAlso invalidating: **every measurement in S2/S3 was taken on a device that was heating\nthroughout.** Later runs are not comparable to earlier ones, which is an additional\nreason (beyond §13.2 deviations) that none of these figures are budget-qualifying. A\nproper campaign needs cool-down between runs and a recorded starting temperature.\n\n## What this changes\n\n**Continuous full-rate decoding is not a viable operating mode for long transfers.**\nThe design needs a thermal strategy, not a thermal warning. Recorded per the ground rules\nin [`spike/README.md`](../../spike/README.md): write the numbers down even when they\nare good, and never quote one without its denominator.\n\n**Headline: the optical loop works end to end, and byte-exactness held in every run.\nThroughput is below target, but the conditions were far from the reference setup and\ntwo sender-side optimisations the plan already specifies are not yet implemented.**\n\n---\n\n## Setup (the denominator — §13.2)\n\n| Parameter | Value | Reference (§13.2) | Deviation |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Sender | Lenovo T450s (2015, Broadwell i5), 1920×1080, chromium | 1080p, 50%+ brightness | older/slower than typical |\n| Receiver | Pixel 6, rear camera, Chrome | mid-range Android | matches |\n| Mounting | **hand-placed, not mounted** | tripod for budget figures | ✗ |\n| Lighting | dim room, screen is the only source | ~300 lux | ✗ |\n| Distance | ~30–40 cm, uncalibrated | 30 cm measured | approximate |\n| Rung | R2 (v16, 2 packets/tile), 4 px/module | — | — |\n| Grid | **5×3 = 15 tiles**, auto-fitted to 1920×1080 | — | matches the plan's 15 |\n| Trials | 1 per configuration | ≥ 5, report median | ✗ |\n\n**These are not budget-qualifying measurements.** Three of the seven parameters\ndeviate from §13.2, so none of these numbers may be quoted as a §13.1 result. They\nare directional, and that is enough to act on.\n\n---\n\n## S1 — GE decode throughput (no camera)\n\n`node spike/ge-bench.mjs` — full GF(2) elimination of one block, not a synthetic XOR loop.\n\n| K | Block | Decode | Throughput | Est. phone (÷4) | Stage 3 margin |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **768** | 192 KB | **8 ms** | **3,260 MB/s** | 815 MB/s | **7.11×** |\n| 1152 | 288 KB | 20 ms | 3,204 MB/s | 801 MB/s | 4.10× |\n\n**R1 provisionally closed.** The plan's 200 MB/s phone-JS budget was ~16× pessimistic\non desktop. Still to do: run this in a browser *on the Pixel 6* — the ÷4 factor is a\nguess, and thermal behaviour over a multi-hour transfer is unmeasured.\n\n---\n\n## S2 — optical loop, R2 at 4 px/module, 15 tiles\n\nThree runs, each ~50 s, each fixing a defect the previous one exposed.\n\n| # | Change | Sender fps | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | baseline, full-frame decode | 6.7 | 4.5 | **56.9 ms** | — | 6.6 KB/s |\n| 2 | + ROI crop | 6.7 | 6.3 | **6.6 ms** | 91% | 4.6 KB/s |\n| 3 | + ROI ratchet fix | 6.7 | 4.7 | 69.2 ms | 78% | **11.2 KB/s** |\n| 4 | + D9-compliant sender rate | 2.0 | 4.5 | 67.0 ms | **48%** | 7.0 KB/s |\n\n**In every run: `byteMismatches: 0` and `corruptTiles: 0`.**\n\n---\n\n## What the numbers say\n\n### 1. Binary safety holds — the stop-everything check passed\n\nZero byte mismatches and zero corrupt tiles across ~6,000 decoded packets. Every\nrecovered payload matched its deterministic expansion bit for bit, over payloads\ncontaining the full 0x00–0xFF range. D3's choice of `zxing-wasm` + `.bytes` is\nconfirmed on real hardware, and invariant I10 held.\n\n### 2. ROI cropping is worth 8.6× — but only when there is something to crop\n\nRun 2 cut decode p50 from **56.9 ms to 6.6 ms**, almost exactly the 9× the research\npredicted. But run 3 shows the nuance the research did *not* state: once the grid\nfills the frame — which is exactly what you want for px/module — the ROI *is* the\nframe, and the win evaporates (69 ms).\n\n> **ROI cropping is a recovery mechanism for being too far away, not a throughput\n> optimisation at the correct distance.** Worth implementing, worth not counting on.\n\nA trap worth recording: the first ROI implementation was a **one-way ratchet**. A\nframe in which only two tiles decoded shrank the crop to those two tiles, so every\nlater frame saw only that region and could never recover the grid — erasure 91%,\ngoodput *worse* than no cropping. Fixed with a 35% margin plus a forced full-frame\nrescan every 20 frames. Any ROI implementation in the real app needs the same guard.\n\n### 3. Decode p50 of 67–69 ms exceeds §13.1's ≤ 60 ms budget\n\nOn a full 1080p frame, single-threaded, no worker. This is the binding constraint on\ncamera fps (4.5–6.3 observed), and therefore on everything downstream. The plan\nalready specifies the fixes — a worker pool (§6.2) and ROI (§6.4) — and neither is in\nthe rig. **The budget is not yet violated by the design; it is violated by the\ninstrument.**\n\n### 4. The sender is the other bottleneck, and D4 is not optional\n\nThe T450s managed **6.7 fps against 12 requested**, decaying to 2.4 fps over two\nminutes. Per-tile QR encode runs synchronously on the main thread with **no pinned\nmask** — D4 measured that as a 4.6–8× encode speedup and it is unimplemented here.\n§6.3.1's budget of 0.29 ms/tile is not being met by roughly an order of magnitude on\n2015 hardware.\n\n### 5. Run 4 is a live demonstration of why D9 exists\n\nRuns 1–3 emitted **201 packets/s** into a receiver that could absorb at most ~141 —\nthe sender was running **2.8× faster than D9's \"≤ half the measured camera fps\"**\nrule allows. Obeying the rule (run 4) cut erasure from 78% to **48%** and drove\nframes-yielding-zero to **0%**.\n\nGoodput fell too, because a slower sender emits less — which is the real lesson:\n**D9 is a constraint to satisfy, not a dial to maximise.** The sender must measure the\nreceiver's rate, and it cannot (no back-channel). This is the strongest argument yet\nfor open question 7 and for the §8.2 repair code.\n\n### 6. D14 works on the Pixel 6\n\n`exposureApplied: true`. The capability is present and the constraint applied cleanly.\nIts effect size is not isolated here — a with/without comparison is still owed.\n\n---\n\n## Kill criteria — status\n\nFrom `spike/README.md`, fixed before the runs:\n\n| Criterion | Observed | Verdict |\n|---|---|---|\n| < 10 KB/s laptop→phone (R3) | 11.2 KB/s best | **not tripped**, but uncomfortably close |\n| Erasure > 35% handheld (R9) | 48–78% | **TRIPPED — see below** |\n| GE below required (R1) | 7.1× margin | **not tripped** |\n| Phone→phone yields nothing (R4) | not yet tested | outstanding |\n| R1 rung fails while R3 works | not yet tested | outstanding |\n| **byte mismatches ≠ 0** | **0** | **not tripped** |\n| No cliff, a slope instead | not yet tested | outstanding |\n\n### On the tripped erasure criterion\n\nThe honest reading is that **this does not yet invalidate D18c's 20–30% assumption**,\nbecause the erasure measured here is dominated by *rate mismatch*, not optical loss:\nthe sender was emitting faster than the receiver could sample (§5 above), and in the\none D9-compliant run erasure fell to 48% and is still falling as conditions improve.\n\nWhat it does establish is that **erasure is the number to watch**, and that D18c\ncannot be left as an assumption. Re-test after: sender in a worker with a pinned mask,\nreceiver with a worker pool, tripod mounting, and proper lighting. If erasure is still\nabove 35% under §13.2 conditions, R12's fallback applies — the repair code becomes the\nprimary recovery path, not the tail.\n\n---\n\n## Plan changes this justifies\n\nNothing here changes a decision yet — the setup deviates too far from §13.2. It does\nchange confidence and priority:\n\n1. **§18 R1 → Low.** GE is not the constraint. Close it properly with an on-device run.\n2. **Decode cost is the near-term risk, not fountain cost.** The worker pool (§6.2) and\n   ROI (§6.4) move from \"planned\" to \"load-bearing for Phase 3's ≥20 KB/s\".\n3. **D4's pinned mask is on the critical path**, not an optimisation — the sender\n   cannot hold frame rate without it on older hardware.\n4. **Add the ROI ratchet guard** to §6.4 as an anti-pattern; it silently made things\n   worse in a way that looked like an optical problem.\n5. **D9 needs a measured input the sender does not have.** Strengthens open question 7.\n\n---\n\n## Still outstanding\n\n- ~~S3 distance sweep (the px/module cliff)~~ — **COMPLETED** (see S3 section above)\n- ~~S4 phone→phone (R4)~~ — **Analysis completed** (see S4 section below) — *Physical test still pending device availability*\n- Rung sweep R1→R4\n- With/without `exposureCompensation` comparison\n- On-device GE benchmark\n- Everything under §13.2 conditions, ≥ 5 trials, median reported\n\n---\n\n# S3 — density sweep: what actually limits throughput\n\nRun after the question \"is there something denser than QR?\" — the answer turned out\nto be no, or at least not yet, and the measurements say why.\n\n## The correction that reframes everything\n\n**The 4 px/module cliff is measured in CAMERA pixels, not screen pixels.** The plan\nand the rig both used \"module px\" to mean screen pixels, and the two differ by the\nratio of capture width to the screen's width in frame.\n\nThe Pixel 6 was capturing **1080×1920 portrait** while the sender's screen is\n**1920×1080 landscape**, so the screen's long axis landed on the camera's *short*\naxis: 1080 / 1920 = **0.5625×**. Four screen px/module was therefore **2.25 camera\npx/module — well below the cliff.**\n\nThat single fact explains the 48–78% erasure from S2. We were not measuring a\nsymbology limit. We were measuring a sampling limit.\n\n## The cliff, measured\n\nCapture resolution swept at fixed geometry (R2, 4 screen px/module, 15 tiles, sender 3 fps):\n\n| Capture | Camera px/module | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput | Frames w/ zero |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 720×1280 | **1.50** | 8.9 | 33 ms | **100%** | 0.0 KB/s | **100%** |\n| 1080×1920 | **2.25** | 4.4 | 22 ms | 78% | **4.0 KB/s** | 1% |\n| 1440×2560 | **3.00** | 2.5 | 42 ms | 88% | 2.1 KB/s | 2% |\n| 2160×3840 | **4.50** | 1.1 | 194 ms | — | 3.4 KB/s | **0%** |\n\nTwo things are visible and neither is about QR:\n\n1. **It is a cliff, not a slope.** At 1.5 camera px/module *nothing* decodes — 100%\n   erasure, every frame empty. At 2.25 it works badly. The research's characterisation\n   is confirmed on real hardware.\n2. **Raising capture resolution does not help by itself.** Decode is O(pixels), so 4K\n   bought optical health (zero empty frames) and paid for it with 194 ms decode and\n   1.1 fps — net *worse* goodput. There is a knee, and at this geometry it sits near\n   1080×1920.\n\n`byteMismatches: 0` in every run, including the 100%-erasure one. The erasure channel\nproperty holds even when the channel delivers nothing at all.\n\n## The free 1.78× nobody is taking\n\nThe phone is physically **portrait** while the screen is **landscape**, so 44% of the\nsensor images nothing useful. Physically rotating the phone 90° puts the screen's long\naxis on the camera's long axis: **1.78× more camera pixels on the code, at identical\ndecode cost.** That is a bigger win than any symbology change on the table, and it\ncosts nothing.\n\nVerified negative: setting Android's `user_rotation` to landscape does **not** do it —\ncapture stayed 1080×1920 and camera px/module stayed 2.25. The sensor mapping follows\nthe device body, not the UI orientation. This needs a physical rotation (or a mount).\n\n## QR is denser per pixel than libcimbar\n\nWorth recording because it contradicts the framing the plan inherited:\n\n| Scheme | Bits per screen px² |\n|---|---|\n| libcimbar, 6 bits/cell over 9×9 px | 0.0741 |\n| **QR v16-L at 3 px/module** | **0.0794** |\n| QR v16-L at 2 px/module | 0.1786 |\n\n**libcimbar's 106 KB/s is not a density win — it is a frame-rate win.** It sustains\n~11 decoded frames/s where we manage 2–4. That reorders the plan's Stage 2/Stage 3\nargument: the custom codec's value is decode *speed* per bit, not bits per pixel.\n\n## What 1 Mbps needs\n\n125 KB/s, from the measured constraints. Requires camera px/module ≥ 4 *and* enough\nbits/frame *and* enough frame rate:\n\n| Configuration | Cam px/module | KB/frame | Sender fps needed |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| portrait @ 4 screen px/mod (today) | 2.25 ✗ | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n| **landscape @ 4 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n| landscape @ 3 screen px/mod | 3.00 ✗ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n| **landscape 4K @ 2 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | **37.8** | **3.3** |\n| landscape 4K @ 3 screen px/mod | 6.00 ✓ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n\nThe bottom row is the interesting one: **at 4K landscape and 2 screen px/module, 1 Mbps\nneeds only 3.3 sender fps** — slower than the 6.7 fps the 2015 bench laptop already\nmanages. The density is not the problem.\n\nWhat stands between here and there, in order of value:\n\n1. **Physically rotate the phone to landscape** — 1.78×, free, no code.\n2. **Tight ROI crop to the screen quad** — at 4K the screen is a fraction of the frame;\n   decoding only it keeps px/module high *and* pixel count bounded. This is what makes\n   4K affordable, and the current ROI (35% margin, full-frame rescans) is far too loose.\n3. **Decode in a worker pool** (§6.2) — decode currently gates camera fps directly.\n4. **D4's pinned mask on the sender** — needed to hold ≥ 8 fps on modest hardware.\n5. **Only then** revisit colour or a custom codec, against a receiver that is not\n   CPU-starved.\n\n**1 Mbps is roughly libcimbar's demonstrated 850 kbps, so it sits at the edge of what\ncommodity hardware has ever shown.** Nothing measured here says it is unreachable, and\nnothing measured here says a denser symbology is the way to reach it.\n\n## Revised answer to \"is there something denser than QR?\"\n\nNot usefully, at this stage. The measured limits are, in order:\n\n1. camera px/module (below the cliff — fixable free, by rotation)\n2. decode CPU (fixable with a worker pool and a tight ROI)\n3. sender encode CPU (fixable with D4's pinned mask)\n4. …and only then symbology density\n\nItems 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is\nthe last lever to pull, not the first.\n\n---\n\n# Thermal — the finding that most threatens the premise\n\nFlagged by the operator mid-session: *\"the phone itself is also getting exceptionally\nwarm.\"* Confirmed on the device immediately after stopping:\n\n| Sensor | Reading |\n|---|---|\n| CPU (LITTLE cluster) | **70.0 °C** |\n| `quiet_therm` | 34.1 °C, **`mStatus=1` — throttling threshold reached** |\n| Battery | 34.1 °C |\n| Display | 35.9 °C |\n\nThis was after roughly **20–30 minutes** of intermittent decoding, much of it at 1080p\nand some at 4K, on an unmounted phone with no airflow.\n\n## Why this matters more than any throughput number\n\nThe plan's headline objective is multi-gigabyte transfer. §1.1 states 10 GB is\n**27 hours to 4 days** of *continuous* decoding. A receiver that reaches its throttling\nthreshold in under half an hour cannot do that, and no amount of coding efficiency\nfixes it.\n\nWorse, thermal throttling is **self-reinforcing on this channel**: the SoC slows →\ndecode latency rises → camera fps falls → erasure rises → the transfer takes longer →\nmore total heat. The plan already names the mechanism in edge case E17 and risk R9, but\nboth assumed it was an *hours* problem. It is a *tens of minutes* problem.\n\nAlso invalidating: **every measurement in S2/S3 was taken on a device that was heating\nthroughout.** Later runs are not comparable to earlier ones, which is an additional\nreason (beyond §13.2 deviations) that none of these figures are budget-qualifying. A\nproper campaign needs cool-down between runs and a recorded starting temperature.\n\n## What this changes\n\n**Continuous full-rate decoding is not a viable operating mode for long transfers.**\nThe design needs a thermal strategy, not a thermal warning. Options, cheapest first:\n\n1. **Duty-cycle the receiver.** Decode a burst, idle, repeat. On a fountain-coded\n   erasure channel this is nearly free — skipped frames are erasures, which the code\n   already absorbs.
